summary: Defines two new actions for the Sieve email filtering language that add and delete header fields in messages. This lets filtering scripts modify the headers of a message, for example to insert a marker for later processing or to remove an unwanted field. It is a standards-track extension.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a mail sorter who can write a label on the envelope or erase one. This lets mail filter rules add or remove the notes at the top of an email.

subtitle: Two Sieve actions that let a mail filter script add header fields to a message and delete them.

tldr.problem: Sieve scripts could test message headers but not change them, so they could not pass information to, or clean up fields from, other components that read header fields.
tldr.mechanism: The editheader extension adds an addheader action that inserts a header field and a deleteheader action that removes matching ones, with rules for how the changes interact with the rest of a script.
tldr.outcome: Scripts can now stamp or strip header fields, at the cost of possible broken DKIM signatures and spoofable header-based decisions. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 5293 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It remains the definition of the Sieve editheader extension.

sections.title: Why Edit Headers in a Filter
sections.content:
Email header fields are, in the RFC's words, a flexible and easy-to-understand means of communication between email processors. A Sieve script, as defined in RFC 5228, can already look at them. This extension lets a script also change them by adding and deleting header fields, so the script can interact with other components that consume or produce those fields.

The extension is announced to a script with the capability string editheader. The RFC uses "header field" in the sense of RFC 2822: a logical line of an email message header.
sections.plainLanguage: A mail filter used to be able to read the notes written on top of an email. Now it can also write new notes or erase old ones.

sections.title: The addheader Action
sections.content:
The usage is addheader [:last] <field-name> <value>. The action adds a header field to the existing message header. If the field name is not a valid 7-bit US-ASCII header field name, the implementation MUST flag an error. The action does not affect Sieve's implicit keep.

If the value is not valid unstructured text, or exceeds a length limit set by the implementation, the implementation MUST either flag an error or encode the value using folding white space and the encodings from RFC 2047 or RFC 2231. An implementation MAY limit the encoded header field's size, but the limit MUST NOT be less than 998 characters, not counting the terminating CRLF.

By default the new field goes at the beginning of the existing header. With the optional :last flag it is appended at the end.
sections.plainLanguage: The filter can write a new note on the envelope. Usually it goes on top of the pile of notes, but you can ask for it to go at the bottom.

sections.title: The deleteheader Action
sections.content:
The usage is deleteheader [:index <fieldno> [:last]] [COMPARATOR] [MATCH-TYPE] <field-name> [<value-patterns>]. By default it deletes all occurrences of the named header field. The field name is mandatory and is always matched as a case-insensitive US-ASCII string. Like addheader, it does not affect the implicit keep.

If value patterns are given, only occurrences whose values match any of them are deleted. Matching follows the chosen match type and comparator, as if by the header test, and leading and trailing whitespace in the field values is ignored. Without value patterns, the comparator and match type are silently ignored.

:index limits the action to one occurrence, counting from 1 for the first. With :last the count runs backwards, so 1 is the last occurrence. Counting happens before the value patterns are applied, so deleteheader :index 1 :contains "Delivered-To" "bob@example.com" deletes the first Delivered-To field if it contains that address, not the first one that does.

It is not an error if nothing matches, or if the index is larger than the number of fields. It is an error to give :last without :index.
sections.plainLanguage: The filter can also erase notes by name. It can erase all of them, only the third one, or only the ones that say something particular.

sections.title: Limits on What Can Change
sections.content:
As local policy, an implementation MAY limit which header fields scripts may add or delete. Two rules are fixed, however: implementations MUST NOT permit deleting Received and Auto-Submitted header fields, and MUST permit both adding and deleting Subject.

If a script attempts a change that is not permitted, the attempt MUST be silently ignored rather than raising an error.
sections.plainLanguage: Some notes are too important to erase, like the stamps showing which post offices a letter went through. The filter is simply not allowed to remove them, and it is not told off for trying.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Sieve Features
sections.content:
Actions that generate delivery status or disposition messages (DSN, MDN) MUST use the original, unmodified header. If an error ends the script, the original header is also used for the implicit keep. Every other action that stores, sends or alters the message uses the current set of header fields, including addheader and deleteheader themselves. So adding X-Hello and then deleting its first occurrence leaves the message unchanged.

Tests such as exists and header, and extensions such as vacation, MUST see the header as modified so far. A header test for X-Hello after adding it will always be true. An implementation MAY ignore changes when a header affects how other parts of the message are parsed, so a body test (see RFC 5173) may be unaffected by edits to Content-Type.

For weeding out duplicates, a message modified by these actions MUST be treated as the same as the original, so keep; addheader "X-Flavor" "vanilla"; keep; files only one message. The implicit keep is thought of as running at the end of the script, after the edits, though a cancelled implicit keep stays cancelled.
sections.plainLanguage: Each rule in the script sees the envelope as it looks right now, with all the notes already added or erased. But if a bounce message has to be sent, it uses the original, untouched envelope.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Someone with write access to a user's script storage could use this extension to generate headers that the user would otherwise be shielded from, for example by a gateway MTA that removes them. A script that removes header fields may also unwisely destroy evidence about the path a message took.

Changing headers can break digital signatures that cover them. Changes to fields in the DKIM list of fields that SHOULD be signed (RFC 4871) can invalidate DKIM signatures, including ones that guarantee a field's absence. S/MIME and OpenPGP signatures are not directly affected, because they keep a separate copy of the headers inside the signed body, though software that compares the inner and outer copies could notice differences. Many signature schemes ignore headers added at the front, so addheader works with them unless :last is used.

Any filter decision based on headers can be spoofed. If a user's script trusts an APPROVED tag, a malicious sender can add it too. One defence is to delete or rename such headers before processing the message.

The RFC also notes that this is the first standardized Sieve extension that alters messages being processed. Combined with a redirect back to the same user, a script could keep some state between runs, but it cannot loop forever because each pass adds a Received field, which the extension is forbidden to alter.
sections.plainLanguage: Erasing or adding notes can break a wax seal that covered them, and a sneaky sender can write a fake note, so a filter should not blindly trust a note it finds.
